newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - Thyssen scales back telecoms plans.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Thyssen scales back telecoms plans.

text.p: Thyssen Telecom, the telecommunications arm of German steel giant Thyssen AG, on Tuesday unveiled a new strategy for entering the hard-fought telecoms market, sharply scaling-back its planned services.

Having lost a major telecoms bid to a rival this year and facing chilly regulatory headwinds, Thyssen has abandoned ambitious goals, choosing instead to focus on mobile phones and take a wait-and-see attitude towards public phone services.

But company officials at a news conference in Duesseldorf said the humble business plan was not the beginning of a full retreat and vehemently dismissed speculation Thyssen could sell its 30.1 percent stake in the E-Plus mobile phone company.
Hans-Erich Forster, Thyssen Telecom chairman, said there was no basis for press reports claiming utility RWE has offered Thyssen 3.5 billion marks ($2.24 billion) for its E-Plus stake.
"Neither Thyssen AG nor Thyssen Telecom have received such an offer. Negotiations are not taking place," he said.
Thyssen Telecom has been under pressure to come up with a new strategy after losing a bid this year for a 49 percent stake in the telecoms subsidiary of the German railway.

The stake in DBKom GmbH went to a group led by engineering firm Mannesmann AG that includes U.S. phone giant AT&T Corp. That left Thyssen alone and without a clear vision of how to compete against monopoly Deutsche Telekom when the market for public phone service opens fully in 1998.

Thyssen commissioned industry consultant Roland Berger to help draft a new strategy for entering the market. The plan puts E-Plus at the top of the company's list of priorities and folds its Internet and other multimedia services into a new company with the name Multimedia Service-Gesellschaft (MSG).
While it leads the E-Plus consortium, other shareholders include Veba, BellSouth and Vodafone.

But Thyssen has scaled back previous plans to enter the public phone services market as a reseller -- selling phone services by leasing network capacity from other carriers -- through its PlusNet corporate communications unit.
Thyssen officials said current legislation regulating access to the networks of Deutsche Telekom made it improbable that resale could be conducted profitably in Germany.
The idea of MSG is not new. Dieter Vogel, now Thyssen group chairman, said two years ago as head of Thyssen Telecom its multimedia activities would be grouped in a separate company.
What appears to be new in Thyssen's strategy is a decision to minimize risks and focus on proven business activities, such as wireless and the growing Internet services business.

After investing some 650 million marks in telecoms so far, Thyssen plans to invest another 700 million marks over the next five years. It sees sales of up to three billion marks by then, including its share E-Plus and the TelMI paging service.
That is a huge change from forecasts made at its 1994 launch when it predicted turnover of 10 billion marks and said it would invest up to four billion marks.

"Focussing on services does not mean we are abandoning the residential market," said Thyssen Telecom managing director Hans-Peter Kohlhammer. "This is a modified strategy to allow us in several years to be present in this market, but profitably."
Thyssen Telecom sales rose to 184.5 million marks in the business year that ended on September 30 from 66.3 million the year before.
